title: Top Down Operator Precedence
why: Crockford's working JavaScript implementation of Pratt parsing, the clearest short statement of the expression(rbp) loop and of infix versus infixr binding powers.

title: Simple but Powerful Pratt Parsing
why: Kladov's from-scratch derivation using left/right binding-power pairs and a min_bp loop, with the pair for a right-associative operator shown explicitly.

title: Pratt Parsing and Precedence Climbing Are the Same Algorithm
why: Chu's argument, from implementing both, that precedence climbing and Pratt parsing are one algorithm described twice.

title: Parsing Expressions by Recursive Descent
version: (C) 1999 with later updates (the derivation section is dated 2013); accessed 2026-10-17
why: Norvell's account of precedence climbing and its history, including who described and invented it and why he coined the name.

claim: Pratt calls the code a token runs when an expression precedes it its left denotation (led), and the code it runs with no preceding expression its null denotation (nud).
quote: We will call the code denoted by a token with (without) a preceding expression its left (null) denotation or led (nud).

locator: section 3, Implementation (parser states q0 and q1)
claim: A Pratt parser fixes a right binding power (rbp) for each recursive call and reads the left binding power (lbp) from the current token, which can change at every step.
quote: In making this call we supply the binding power associated with the desired argument, which we call the rbp (right binding power), whose value remains fixed as this incarnation of the parser runs. The lbp (left binding power) is a property of the current token in the input stream, and in general will change each time state q1 is entered.

locator: Infix Operators (the infix and infixr led functions, with the expression loop while (rbp < token.lbp))
claim: Crockford's ordinary infix led calls expression(bp) for the right operand and so is left-associative, while infixr calls expression(bp - 1), reducing the right binding power and making the operator right-associative.
quote: Those infix operators are left associative. We can also make right associative operators, such as short-circuiting logical operators, by reducing the right binding power.

claim: Kladov gives each infix operator a left and a right binding power; the right-associative '.' is the pair (6, 5), and he says the left side binding tighter is what gives right associativity.
quote: Note how the left side of the operator binds tighter, which gives us desired right associativity

claim: Norvell says Keith Clarke proved the method correct by program transformation in a 1985 report, and that Martin Richards appears to have invented it first for CPL and BCPL.
quote: Keith gives a proof of its correctness, relative to the classic algorithm, by means of program transformation in a 1985 report "The top-down parsing of expressions" [0]. The algorithm appears to have been first invented by Martin Richards for use in the CPL and BCPL compilers.

locator: Background, paragraph after the TDOP implementation description
claim: Chu says that after implementing the richer arithmetic language with TDOP he realized precedence climbing and Pratt parsing are the same algorithm.
quote: In doing so, I realized that Precedence climbing and Pratt parsing are the same algorithm.

claim: Pratt presented "Top Down Operator Precedence" at the first annual Principles of Programming Languages Symposium in Boston in 1973.
